## Foot's original

Philippa Foot, "The Problem of Abortion and the Doctrine of the Double Effect", *Oxford Review* no. 5, 1967. The trolley is a side example in a paper about something else. Her version: the driver of a tram whose brakes have failed can steer onto a track where one man is working instead of the track with five. Most people say he should steer. Foot's point was the difference between doing and allowing, and between what you intend and what you merely foresee.

## Thomson's footbridge

Judith Jarvis Thomson renamed it "the trolley problem" in "Killing, Letting Die, and the Trolley Problem", *The Monist*, 1976, and returned to it in the *Yale Law Journal* in 1985. She moved the chooser off the tram and onto the bank by a lever, then onto a footbridge above the track beside a large man. Push him and his body stops the trolley. Same arithmetic, five against one, and almost nobody will push.

The loop variant (the side track loops back, so the one man's body is what stops it) is the one that breaks students' rules of thumb.

## My TY poll, 7 November 2024

27 students, hands up, eyes closed so nobody copies.

| Case | Pull or push | Refuse |
|---|---|---|
| Lever | 23 | 4 |
| Footbridge | 3 | 24 |
| Loop | 14 | 13 |

Ciara's objection to the footbridge: "You don't know he's heavy enough, sir." Fair. That's the problem with thought experiments: the stipulations do all the work. Darragh asked whether it changes if the man on the bridge is the one who cut the brakes. It does, for nearly everyone, which got us onto desert and responsibility (and from there to [[Free will debate]]).

## Moral Machine

Awad et al., "The Moral Machine experiment", *Nature*, November 2018. About 40 million decisions from people in 233 countries and territories, all about self-driving cars choosing whom to hit. Strong preferences for sparing humans over pets, more lives over fewer, the young over the old. Big cultural clusters, e.g. weaker preference for sparing the young in some East Asian samples. See [[Ethics of AI]].

## Where I land

Not a consequentialist, which surprises my brother. The doctrine of double effect goes back to Aquinas, *Summa* II-II q.64 a.7, on killing in self-defence. I think the lever is permissible and the push isn't, and I can't fully say why, which is exactly where [[Utilitarianism]] gets its grip.
